title: Habakkuk

stories.title: 📣 Habakkuk 1
summaryBullets: This is the burden that Habakkuk the prophet received in a vision: (1:1).
How long, O LORD, must I call for help but You do not hear, or cry out to You, “Violence!” but You do not save? (1:2).
Why do You make me see iniquity? Why do You tolerate wrongdoing? Destruction and violence are before me. Strife is ongoing, and conflict abounds. (1:3).
Therefore the law is paralyzed, and justice never goes forth. For the wicked hem in the righteous, so that justice is perverted. (1:4).
“Look at the nations and observe— be utterly astounded! For I am doing a work in your days that you would never believe even if someone told you. (1:5).
For behold, I am raising up the Chaldeans — that ruthless and impetuous nation which marches through the breadth of the earth to seize dwellings not their own. (1:6).
They are dreaded and feared; from themselves they derive justice and sovereignty. (1:7).
Their horses are swifter than leopards, fiercer than wolves of the night. Their horsemen charge ahead, and their cavalry comes from afar. They fly like a vulture, swooping down to devour. (1:8).
All of them come bent on violence; their hordes advance like the east wind; they gather prisoners like sand. (1:9).
They scoff at kings and make rulers an object of scorn. They laugh at every fortress and build up siege ramps to seize it. (1:10).
Then they sweep by like the wind and pass through. They are guilty; their own strength is their god.” (1:11).
Are You not from everlasting, O LORD, my God, my Holy One? We will not die. O LORD, You have appointed them to execute judgment; O Rock, You have established them for correction. (1:12).

Your eyes are too pure to look upon evil, and You cannot tolerate wrongdoing. So why do You tolerate the faithless? Why are You silent while the wicked swallow up those more righteous than themselves? (1:13).
You have made men like the fish of the sea, like creeping things that have no ruler. (1:14).
The foe pulls all of them up with a hook; he catches them in his dragnet, and gathers them in his fishing net; so he rejoices gladly. (1:15).
Therefore he sacrifices to his dragnet and burns incense to his fishing net, for by these things his portion is sumptuous and his food is rich. (1:16).
Will he, therefore, empty his net and continue to slay nations without mercy? (1:17).
crossRefs: 2 Kings 24:1-4: Babylon’s rise against Judah (historical backdrop).
Jeremiah 5:26-31: Violence and twisted justice in Judah.
Deuteronomy 28:49-52: A swift nation as judgment.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כַּשְׂדִּים (Kasdîm), Greek (LXX): Χαλδαῖοι, Aramaic: כשדאי (Kashday)
translationNotes.note: Ethnic/political name for the Neo-Babylonian power (1:6).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חָמָס (ḥāmās), Greek (LXX): ἀδικία/βία, Aramaic: חמס
translationNotes.note: Wrongdoing/violence; frequent in (1:2-3) unrelated to modern political uses of the word.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: תָּפֻג (tafug, ‘go numb’), Greek (LXX): ἀπεκοιμήθη (‘has slept’), Aramaic: אתרפי (‘is slack’)
Hebrew: וַיִּצְבֹּר עָפָר (vayyitsbor ʿāfār), Greek (LXX): συνάξει χοῦν, Aramaic: וכנש עפרא
translationNotes.note: Siege ramps piled to breach city walls (1:10).

stories.keyTakeaway: Habakkuk protests local injustice; God replies that He will use the Babylonians as His instrument of judgment.

stories.title: 🕰️ Habakkuk 2
summaryBullets: I will stand at my guard post and station myself on the ramparts. I will watch to see what He will say to me, and how I should answer when corrected. (2:1).
Then the LORD answered me: “Write down this vision and clearly inscribe it on tablets, so that a herald may run with it. (2:2).
For the vision awaits an appointed time; it testifies of the end and does not lie. Though it lingers, wait for it, since it will surely come and will not delay. (2:3).
Look at the proud one; his soul is not upright — but the righteous will live by faith — (2:4).

and wealth indeed betrays him. He is an arrogant man never at rest. He enlarges his appetite like Sheol, and like Death, he is never satisfied. He gathers all the nations to himself and collects all the peoples as his own. (2:5).

Will not all of these take up a taunt against him, speaking with mockery and derision: ‘Woe to him who amasses what is not his and makes himself rich with many loans! How long will this go on?’ (2:6).
Will not your creditors suddenly arise and those who disturb you awaken? Then you will become their prey. (2:7).
Because you have plundered many nations, the remnant of the people will plunder you— because of your bloodshed against man and your violence against the land, the city, and all their dwellers. (2:8).
Woe to him who builds his house by unjust gain, to place his nest on high and escape the hand of disaster! (2:9).
You have plotted shame for your house by cutting off many peoples and forfeiting your life. (2:10).
For the stones will cry out from the wall, and the rafters will echo it from the woodwork. (2:11).
Woe to him who builds a city with bloodshed and establishes a town by iniquity! (2:12).
Is it not indeed from the LORD of Hosts that the labor of the people only feeds the fire, and the nations weary themselves in vain? (2:13).
For the earth will be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD as the waters cover the sea. (2:14).
Woe to him who gives drink to his neighbors, pouring it from the wineskin until they are drunk, in order to gaze at their nakedness! (2:15).

You will be filled with shame instead of glory. You too must drink and expose your uncircumcision! The cup in the LORD’s right hand will come around to you, and utter disgrace will cover your glory. (2:16).

For your violence against Lebanon will overwhelm you, and the destruction of animals will terrify you, because of your bloodshed against men and your violence against the land, the city, and all their dwellers. (2:17).
What use is an idol, that a craftsman should carve it — or an image, a teacher of lies? For its maker trusts in his own creation; he makes idols that cannot speak. (2:18).
Woe to him who says to wood, ‘Awake!’ or to silent stone, ‘Arise!’ Can it give guidance? Behold, it is overlaid with gold and silver, yet there is no breath in it at all.” (2:19).
But the LORD is in His holy temple; let all the earth be silent before Him. (2:20).
crossRefs: Isaiah 8:1: Write on a tablet, plain and large (public message).
Daniel 8:19: Vision for an appointed time.
Romans 1:17; Galatians 3:11; Hebrews 10:37-38: Later citations of Habakkuk 2:4-3.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: לַמּוֹעֵד (la-moʿed), Greek (LXX): εἰς καιρόν, Aramaic: לזמנא

translationNotes.term: The righteous will live by his faith/faithfulness
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בֶּאֱמוּנָתוֹ (be’emunato), Greek (LXX): ἐκ πίστεως, Aramaic: בהימנותיה/בקיומיה
translationNotes.note: ’Emunah conveys firmness/steadfastness; statement about how the righteous live (2:4).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הִנֵּה עֻפְּלָה לֹא־יָשְׁרָה נַפְשׁוֹ (ʿuplah… lo yashrah nafsho); Greek (LXX): ἐὰν ὑποστείληται…

translationNotes.note: The Old Testament realm of the dead; a shadowy underworld where both righteous and wicked descend (Genesis 37:35; Psalm 16:10). Not necessarily a place of torment; more a state of cessation and silence. The Septuagint and New Testament render it with the Greek word hades.

stories.keyTakeaway: Habakkuk challenges God about Babylon; God commands the vision to be written, promises its set time, and contrasts the proud with the righteous who live by faithfulness.

stories.title: 🎶 Habakkuk 3
summaryBullets: This is a prayer of Habakkuk the prophet, according to Shigionoth: (3:1).
O LORD, I have heard the report of You; I stand in awe, O LORD, of Your deeds. Revive them in these years; make them known in these years. In Your wrath, remember mercy! (3:2).
God came from Teman, and the Holy One from Mount Paran. Selah His glory covered the heavens, and His praise filled the earth. (3:3).
His radiance was like the sunlight; rays flashed from His hand, where His power is hidden. (3:4).
Plague went before Him, and fever followed in His steps. (3:5).
He stood and measured the earth; He looked and startled the nations; the ancient mountains crumbled; the perpetual hills collapsed. His ways are everlasting. (3:6).
I saw the tents of Cushan in distress; the curtains of Midian were trembling. (3:7).
Were You angry at the rivers, O LORD? Was Your wrath against the streams? Did You rage against the sea when You rode on Your horses, on Your chariots of salvation? (3:8).
You brandished Your bow; You called for many arrows. Selah You split the earth with rivers. (3:9).
The mountains saw You and quaked; torrents of water swept by. The deep roared with its voice and lifted its hands on high. (3:10).
Sun and moon stood still in their places at the flash of Your flying arrows, at the brightness of Your shining spear. (3:11).
You marched across the earth with fury; You threshed the nations in wrath. (3:12).
You went forth for the salvation of Your people, to save Your anointed. You crushed the head of the house of the wicked and stripped him from head to toe. Selah (3:13).
With his own spear You pierced his head, when his warriors stormed out to scatter us, gloating as though ready to secretly devour the weak. (3:14).
You trampled the sea with Your horses, churning the great waters. (3:15).

I heard and trembled within; my lips quivered at the sound. Decay entered my bones; I trembled where I stood. Yet I must wait patiently for the day of distress to come upon the people who invade us. (3:16).

Though the fig tree does not bud and no fruit is on the vines, though the olive crop fails and the fields produce no food, though the sheep are cut off from the fold and no cattle are in the stalls, (3:17).
yet I will exult in the LORD; I will rejoice in the God of my salvation! (3:18).
GOD the Lord is my strength; He makes my feet like those of a deer; He makes me walk upon the heights! For the choirmaster. With stringed instruments. (3:19).
crossRefs: Deuteronomy 33:2: The LORD from Sinai/Paran (theophany geography).
Micah 1:3-4: The LORD comes down and mountains melt.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שִׁגְיֹנוֹת (shigyonot), Greek (LXX): ᾠδή/μελῳδία (var.), Aramaic: שגיונות
translationNotes.note: Musical/metrical direction in the psalm heading (3:1).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: תֵּימָן / פָּארָן (Teman/Paran), Greek (LXX): Θαιμάν / Φαράν, Aramaic: תימן / פארן
translationNotes.note: Southern regions linked with Sinai theophany (3:3).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: קַרְנַיִם מִיָּדוֹ (qarnayim miyado), Greek (LXX): ἀκτῖνες, Aramaic: קרנין
translationNotes.note: Image of shining beams (not animal horns) radiating from God’s power (3:4).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: סֶלָה (selah), Greek (trad.): διάψαλμα, Aramaic: סלה

translationNotes.term: He makes my feet like the deer’s
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כְּאַיָּלוֹת (ke’ayyālōt), Greek (LXX): ὡς ἔλαφος, Aramaic: כאילתא

stories.keyTakeaway: Habakkuk sings a temple-style prayer recalling God’s past mighty acts, waits for the coming day, and resolves to rejoice in God even when everything fails.

intro:
Habakkuk was written by Habakkuk the prophet (Habakkuk 1:1; 3:1), of whom no patronymic, village, or other biographical detail is recorded in Scripture beyond his name and prophetic office. The musical notations in chapter 3 ("To the choirmaster: with stringed instruments," Habakkuk 3:19), which mark that section as a psalm intended for liturgical performance, have led many traditional commentators to conclude that Habakkuk was a Levite temple musician, an officer of the worship guild at the Jerusalem temple. The book was composed between 612 BC and 605 BC, after the fall of Nineveh to the Babylonian-Median coalition (612 BC, which Habakkuk does not mention as future) but before the Babylonian invasion of Judah, which Habakkuk prophesies as imminent (Habakkuk 1:5-11; 2:1; 3:16). This places his ministry in the early reign of King Jehoiakim of Judah (609-598 BC), the puppet king installed by Pharaoh Necho II after Necho killed the reforming King Josiah at Megiddo in 609 BC (2 Kings 23:29-35; 2 Chronicles 35:20-36:4). Habakkuk was a contemporary of Jeremiah (the older prophet ministering in Jerusalem) and Daniel (the younger contemporary who would be deported to Babylon in 605 BC during Habakkuk's lifetime). The prophet's name Chavakkuk (חֲבַקּוּק) is of uncertain etymology; it may derive from a Hebrew verbal root meaning "to embrace" (chavaq) or from an Akkadian word for a garden plant. The deuterocanonical addition to Daniel known as Bel and the Dragon (preserved in the Greek Septuagint Daniel chapter 14, found in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles but not in Protestant canons) describes "Habakkuk the prophet" being transported by an angel from Judah to Babylon to feed Daniel in the lions' den; whether this is the same Habakkuk as the canonical prophet, or a different figure with the same name, is unresolved.

The historical setting is the dramatic transition of Near Eastern power from Assyria to Babylon and the corresponding decline of Judah's independence. Assyria had fallen in 612 BC when Nineveh was destroyed; the surviving Assyrian forces regrouped at Haran but were defeated there in 609 BC. Egypt under Pharaoh Necho II (610-595 BC) marched north to support the dying Assyrian state against Babylon, killing the reforming Judahite king Josiah at Megiddo in 609 BC (2 Kings 23:29-30) when Josiah tried to block the Egyptian advance. Necho deposed Josiah's son Jehoahaz after a three-month reign and installed Jehoahaz's brother Eliakim as a puppet king under the throne name Jehoiakim (2 Kings 23:31-35), exacting heavy tribute from Judah. The Babylonians under Nabopolassar and his son Nebuchadnezzar pursued the Egyptians and crushed them at the Battle of Carchemish on the Euphrates in 605 BC, ending Egyptian ambitions in the Levant and bringing all of Syria and Palestine under Babylonian control. Nebuchadnezzar immediately marched south, and Daniel and other young Judahite nobles were taken to Babylon in the first deportation in 605 BC (Daniel 1:1-6). Habakkuk's prophecy that God would raise up the Babylonians (Habakkuk 1:5-11) was fulfilled within years of its delivery.

Habakkuk is the thirty-fifth book of the Christian Old Testament and the eighth of the twelve Minor Prophets. The Hebrew name Chavakkuk (חֲבַקּוּק) is the prophet's own name. Hebrew manuscript fragments of Habakkuk were among the Dead Sea Scrolls discovered at Qumran (mid-20th century AD), preserved as part of the Twelve Minor Prophets scrolls; Qumran cave 1 also yielded a separate Hebrew pesher commentary on Habakkuk chapters 1-2 (1QpHab, the "Habakkuk Pesher"), one of the seven original Dead Sea Scrolls discovered in 1947 and dating to the 1st century BC, which interprets Habakkuk's oracles as applying to the Qumran community's own conflict with the Jerusalem priesthood. Habakkuk 2:4 ("the righteous shall live by his faith") is quoted three times in the New Testament: by Paul in Romans 1:17 and Galatians 3:11, and by the writer of Hebrews in Hebrews 10:38.
